name: Painful legs and moving toes syndrome

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / movement disorder literature
clinicalPearls: A syndrome of deep, poorly localised pain in the leg accompanied by continuous involuntary writhing or flexion-extension movements of the toes or foot
The pain usually dominates the clinical picture and the movements may be only partially suppressible
It often follows injury to peripheral nerves, roots or the cauda equina, though many cases are idiopathic
An analogous painful arms and moving fingers variant is recognised in the upper limb
The movements persist during rest and may reduce but not always disappear in sleep
It is frequently refractory, and management focuses on neuropathic pain control with variable success
reference.pathophysiology: Painful legs and moving toes syndrome is thought to result from aberrant reorganisation of sensory input after peripheral nerve, root or plexus injury, generating abnormal central processing that produces both neuropathic pain and disordered motor output to the toes. The exact generator is uncertain and may involve spinal and supraspinal reorganisation, which is why the movements can be difficult to localise or suppress. In idiopathic cases no antecedent lesion is identified despite a similar clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Dystonia or myoclonus of the foot
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the combination of leg pain and continuous toe movements
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to identify peripheral nerve or root injury
Imaging of the lumbosacral spine or plexus where a lesion is suspected
Exclusion of restless legs syndrome by history
redFlags: Progressive weakness or sensory loss suggesting an evolving lesion
New cauda equina or radicular signs
Rapidly progressive or asymmetric neurological features
reference.prognosis: The syndrome tends to be chronic and often treatment-resistant, with the pain being the most disabling component; some patients gain partial relief from neuropathic pain treatments.
pitfalls: Confusing it with restless legs syndrome, which has an urge to move relieved by movement
Overlooking a treatable peripheral nerve or root lesion
Focusing on the movements rather than the dominant pain
Expecting complete resolution and under-supporting the patient
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Neuropathic pain control with a gabapentinoid such as gabapentin or pregabalin and a tricyclic or SNRI antidepressant such as amitriptyline or duloxetine
Identify and treat any underlying peripheral nerve, root or cauda equina lesion
Botulinum toxin injection to the affected muscles to reduce the involuntary toe movements, with trials of baclofen or a benzodiazepine for the movement component
Adjunctive sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine and consideration of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation or sympathetic and peripheral nerve blocks for refractory pain
Spinal cord stimulation in selected patients with intractable pain
Physiotherapy and multidisciplinary pain-clinic input, addressing comorbid sleep disturbance and low mood, with realistic expectations given the treatment-resistant course
